title: IBM Observes Quantum Chaos-to-Order Phase Transition on 100 Qubits
source_used: Rutgers University news release (9 Oct 2026) and Interesting Engineering; XenoSpectrum original blocked (HTTP 403)
key_facts: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions, in a study published in Nature Physics, showed a quantum computer can repeatedly check and reset parts of itself while running.
The experiment used an IBM Quantum Heron processor with 156 qubits, selecting a connected chain of up to 100 qubits.
The machine alternated between a scrambling step that spread chaos among neighbouring qubits and a control step that measured and reset individual qubits.
The run used nearly 5,000 two-qubit operations and nearly 5,000 checks and resets, which the researchers call the largest successful demonstration of this approach to date.

When scrambling took place more than half the time the system stayed chaotic; when checking and resetting dominated, the qubits could be steered to an orderly state; near an even split a small change flipped the whole system, a phase transition.
The transition became sharper in larger systems and matched theory; the team tested systems of up to 100 qubits against roughly two dozen that conventional computers can simulate.

Jedediah Pixley of Rutgers calls the experiment a landmark on the road to a fault-tolerant quantum computer; IBM's Maika Takita says present-day hardware can coordinate operations, measurements and resets thousands of times across a large system.
Interesting Engineering adds that the demonstration does not establish a fully fault-tolerant quantum computer.
quote_evidence: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.
The researchers conducted the experiment on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron processor, one of the most powerful quantum processors in the world, selecting a connected chain of as many as 100 qubits.
Overall, the team performed nearly 5,000 operations that linked pairs of qubits, along with nearly 5,000 checks and resets.
why_it_matters_hint: Running measurement and reset steps thousands of times on a 100-qubit chip is the kind of real-time feedback that error-corrected quantum computers will need, though it is still a step and not a fault-tolerant machine.
